query: A supplier from a WTO Government Procurement Agreement country is worried that if it loses out on one of our contracts, it will only get whatever review process our domestic courts happen to offer. Is there an internationally guaranteed minimum standard of review it's entitled to, and does the UK's normal court-based challenge route actually satisfy it?

evidence_requirements.description: Article XVIII GPA sets an international-law floor for domestic review procedures: a timely, effective, transparent, non-discriminatory review before at least one impartial and independent authority, with a minimum 10-day period to prepare a challenge, disclosure and a right to be heard, and a timely written and reasoned decision.

The UK gives effect to this floor for treaty state suppliers through its ordinary domestic civil enforcement route: s.100 PA2023 makes the Part 9 duty enforceable by, among others, treaty state suppliers before the High Court (Court of Session in Scotland) - the same court-based route used by UK suppliers - and this court-based model is a recognised, GPA-compliant approach used alongside independent-review-body and tribunal models adopted by other GPA parties.

reference_answer: Article XVIII of the GPA requires every party to provide a timely, effective, transparent and non-discriminatory administrative or judicial review procedure, before at least one impartial authority independent of the procuring entities, giving suppliers no less than 10 days to prepare a challenge, a right to a written response and disclosure of relevant documents, a right to be heard and represented, and a timely, written, reasoned decision. In the UK this floor is given effect domestically because s.100 PA2023 makes the Part 9 procurement duty enforceable in civil proceedings brought by, among others, treaty state suppliers (before the High Court, or Court of Session in Scotland), which is the same two-tier court-based review route (Administrative Court/TCC and appeal courts) used for domestic suppliers. Comparative work by the Procurement Lawyers Association confirms that this traditional UK court model is only one of several models (alongside independent-review-body and tribunal models used by other GPA states such as Canada, Japan and Singapore) that GPA signatories use to meet Article XVIII, and that no particular model is treated as more compliant than another.

topic: Modifying a contract when a known risk materialises
scenario_text: On a major infrastructure contract, ground conditions we flagged in the tender notice as a possible problem have now actually caused delays that mean the contract can't be delivered as planned. Can we modify it to deal with this, and how do we make sure the change won't be successfully challenged?

reference_answer: Schedule 8, paragraph 5 of the Procurement Act 2023 permits a modification where a 'known risk' has materialised (through no fault of either party), the contract can no longer be performed to the authority's satisfaction as a result, the modification goes no further than necessary to remedy that, awarding a new contract instead would not be in the public interest, and (generally) the modification does not increase the contract's estimated value by more than 50%. Paragraph 6 defines a 'known risk' as one the authority identified in the tender or transparency notice as capable of jeopardising performance but incapable of being addressed in the awarded contract. The Act does not say how to draft that notice wording safely. The Cabinet Office's short guide on this ground fills the gap: it recommends identifying likely known risks up front (via lessons learned, NAO/PAC reports, preliminary market engagement, etc.), warns against using the ground as a 'backdoor' for ordinary contract changes that should have been priced in (which invites successful challenge from other bidders), and gives model wording for the tender notice that expressly reserves the right to rely on Schedule 8 paragraph 5 and lists the specific known risks - such as site surveys revealing unforeseen ground conditions.

topic: Contract termination rights following a substantial modification (PCR2015 saved procurement)

query: We awarded a Public Contracts Regulations 2015 contract a couple of years ago, and the incumbent supplier has just agreed a fairly significant change to scope and price with us. If that change turns out to be a 'substantial modification' that should really have gone back out to tender, what termination rights does our contract need to have had in place for this, and what should we actually do now to close things out properly?

evidence_requirements.description: Under PCR 2015, a public contract must contain (or have implied into it) termination rights exercisable where the contract has been subject to a substantial modification of the kind that would have required a new procurement procedure.

Once a regulation 73(1) termination ground has arisen, the practical workflow step is to terminate strictly in accordance with the termination provisions (express or implied) stipulated in the contract itself, not via a separate ad hoc process.

reference_answer: Regulation 73 PCR 2015 requires every public contract to contain provisions letting the contracting authority terminate where (a) the contract has been subject to a substantial modification that would have required a new procurement procedure under regulation 72(9), (b) the contractor should have been excluded at award under regulation 57(1)/(2), or (c) the CJEU has declared a serious Treaty infringement in the award. Regulation 72(8) defines when a modification is 'substantial' (e.g. it materially changes the character of the contract, would have let in other bidders, or shifts the economic balance in the contractor's favour); regulation 72(9) then requires a new procurement procedure for any modification outside the permitted grounds in regulation 72(1)-(7). If the contract does not expressly contain the regulation 73 termination provisions, a power to terminate on reasonable notice is implied into it by regulation 73(3). Practically, the Procurement Journey / Procurement Pathway 'Termination of contracts' guidance confirms that once one of these regulation 73(1) triggers has crystallised, the contracting authority should not invent a new process: termination must be carried out strictly in accordance with whatever termination provisions (express or implied) are stipulated in the contract itself, including any notice-of-termination and consequential-matters provisions it contains.

The Procurement Pathway 'Payment of undisputed invoices within 30 days' guidance operationalises this: contracting authorities should check the contract for these clauses (unless exempt), have regard to any Cabinet Office guidance on the regulation, and be aware that the equivalent implied payment terms now sit in Procurement Act 2023 sections 68 (main contract) and 73 (subcontracts) - i.e. the underlying 30-day prompt-payment duty continues across the PCR2015-to-PA2023 transition, so the same practical check (are the flow-down terms actually in the contract and are invoices being verified promptly) applies regardless of which regime technically governs this particular contract.

Section 71 then imposes ongoing duties: at least once every twelve months during the contract's life, and again on termination, the authority must assess performance against the KPIs and publish the specified information about that assessment. Separately, if a breach results in termination, damages or a settlement, or if the supplier is failing to perform and has been given a fair chance to improve but hasn't, the authority must publish specified information about that within 30 days. So yes, routine annual KPI reporting and reporting a serious performance failure both use the contract performance notice mechanism - but a full termination is reported via a different notice.

Whether this particular emergency actually satisfies all four is a judgement call the officer must make on the facts - it cannot simply be assumed. Finally, once evaluation is complete, a recommendations report should be produced - summarising the process, any supplier disqualifications, the recommendation of award, risks and mitigation, sustainability/Community Benefits considerations - and taken through the organisation's governance arrangements for approval to proceed.

If a variation, extension or amendment is needed, it must go through a structured process - using a Contract Variation Request Form - that documents what changed, why, who approved it, when it was implemented and the cost/scope/delivery impact, because even a low-value contract change must be authorised, documented and compliant with governance rules to avoid disputes or invalid changes. Finally, for dispute resolution, termination or exit: escalate issues early to procurement or legal, follow the dispute resolution procedure set out in the contract, and document the exit strategy and reasons. Throughout, the guidance stresses proportionality - a basic contract management plan/record (key contacts, deliverables, review schedule, expiry date) and simple performance logging are normally sufficient for a contract below the regulated procurement threshold with limited business criticality, rather than the fuller CSM regime used for higher-value or higher-risk (Route 2/3) contracts.

In practice this repeat-purchase justification is only available where the earlier competitively tendered contract's tender documents disclosed the intended follow-on at the outset, and the follow-on must generally be made within 5 years of the original award - a practical eligibility check the bare modified statutory wording does not spell out in plain terms.

Because the earlier contract was actually awarded under PCR2015, regulation 6 of SI 2024/716 modifies paragraph 8 (and the definitions in paragraph 9) so that the reference to a 'competitive tendering procedure' is instead read as a reference to regulation 26(1) and (2) of PCR2015, and the disclosure condition is read as a reference to the disclosure required by regulation 32(11) of PCR2015. Official direct-award guidance explains the underlying justification in practical terms: it is only available where the original competitively tendered contract's tender documents disclosed the intended follow-on as soon as the original contract was put out to tender, and the follow-on must generally be made within 5 years of the original award - so the authority must check the original PCR2015 tender documents for that disclosure and confirm it is still within time, not simply apply the plain PA2023 wording of paragraph 8 unmodified.

Official debarment guidance explains the general notification-of-exclusion expectations (who to notify, and that a challenge must also be notified) that this PSR-specific duty parallels.

reference_answer: Under new reg 20C of the Health Care Services (Provider Selection Regime) Regulations 2023 — inserted by SI 2025/163 reg 28 — where a relevant authority has excluded an excluded/excludable provider (or a subcontractor has been replaced under reg 20A) because it was excluded/excludable under a ground equivalent to s.57(1)(a)/(2)(a) PA2023 or by virtue of being on the national security debarment list, the authority must notify a Minister of the Crown, including where the decision is challenged or subject to review/appeal proceedings, within 30 days of the exclusion and again within 30 days of the challenge starting and of its outcome. This mirrors — for the PSR regime — the general PA2023 debarment notification expectations that GOV.UK debarment guidance describes for the mainstream regime (notifying a Minister of the Crown, the Welsh Ministers or a Northern Ireland department of exclusions and of any challenge).

topic: Defence authority designation for threshold purposes
scenario_text: AWE plc is helping us scope a defence-related contract. For the purposes of applying the Procurement Act's defence and security threshold, is AWE actually treated as a 'defence authority', or does that label only apply to the MOD itself?
query: AWE plc is helping us scope a defence-related contract. For the purposes of applying the Procurement Act's defence and security threshold, is AWE actually treated as a 'defence authority', or does that label only apply to the MOD itself?

evidence_requirements.description: PA2023 defines defence and security contracts and expressly delegates the identification of 'defence authorities' to regulations, without naming any authority itself.
PR2024 reg 46 is the only source that actually names which bodies count as a defence authority, including AWE plc.

reference_answer: AWE plc is treated as a defence authority. Section 7(5) PA2023 leaves the question of which contracting authorities count as a 'defence authority' (relevant to how the defence and security threshold in Schedule 1 applies) to regulations. Regulation 46 of the Procurement Regulations 2024 specifies, for the purposes of s.7(5), that the Secretary of State for Defence, AWE PLC, the National Crime Agency, and the Oil and Pipelines Agency are each a defence authority. The Act's own text does not name any of these bodies — the list exists only in the secondary legislation.

scenario_text: For threshold purposes, if we're procuring installation of new drainage as part of a wider job, is that treated as a 'works' contract? Where do I actually find what counts as 'works'?
query: For threshold purposes, if we're procuring installation of new drainage as part of a wider job, is that treated as a 'works' contract? Where do I actually find what counts as 'works'?

evidence_requirements.description: PA2023 leaves the definition of 'works' (relevant to threshold classification) to regulations rather than defining it itself.
PR2024 reg 45 and Schedule 3 supply the actual, CPV-code-based definition of 'works' that the Act's threshold Schedule depends on.

reference_answer: PA2023 Schedule 1, paragraph 5(1) states that 'works' has the meaning given by regulations, rather than defining it in the Act itself. Regulation 45 of the Procurement Regulations 2024 supplies that meaning: 'works' means any activity that falls within a CPV code listed in Schedule 3 to PR2024. Schedule 3 is a long list of specific CPV codes (e.g. construction work, site preparation, demolition, and — subject to checking the actual code — likely a drainage/pipeline installation code); the query cannot be answered definitively without checking whether the specific drainage activity's CPV code appears in Schedule 3, so this is answerable only with the assumption that the described drainage work falls under one of the listed construction-related CPV codes.

topic: Light touch services and reservation to public service mutuals
scenario_text: We want to run a competitive flexible procedure for a supply-of-nursing-staff contract and restrict it to public service mutuals only. Is nursing staff supply actually eligible to be reserved this way, and where's that confirmed?
query: We want to run a competitive flexible procedure for a supply-of-nursing-staff contract and restrict it to public service mutuals only. Is nursing staff supply actually eligible to be reserved this way, and where's that confirmed?

evidence_requirements.description: PA2023 creates the light touch contract concept (s.9(1)) and the power to reserve light touch contracts to public service mutuals (s.33(7)), without itself specifying which services qualify.

PR2024 reg 42 and Schedule 1 Table 1 are the only source specifying which CPV-coded services are light touch and, separately, which of those are reservable ('R') to public service mutuals — including nursing staff supply.

reference_answer: Yes. Section 9(1) PA2023 defines 'light touch contract' by reference to services specified in regulations, and s.33(7) allows reserving award of light touch contracts (of 5 years or less) to qualifying public service mutuals. Neither section itself lists which services qualify. Regulation 42 PR2024 specifies that services covered by the CPV codes in Schedule 1, Table 1 are light touch services for s.9(1) purposes, and that services in Table 1 marked 'R' are reservable to public service mutuals under s.33(7). Schedule 1, Table 1 lists CPV code 79624000 'Supply services of nursing personnel' with an 'R' marking, confirming it is both a light touch service and reservable to public service mutuals.

topic: Devolved Scottish authority application of PA2023 via inserted s.115A
scenario_text: We're a Scottish health board (a devolved Scottish authority) planning to run a framework jointly with an English NHS trust, using a UK-wide reserved procurement arrangement. I thought the Procurement Act doesn't apply to us as a devolved Scottish authority — does it apply here because we're procuring jointly with an English body?
query: We're a Scottish health board (a devolved Scottish authority) planning to run a framework jointly with an English NHS trust, using a UK-wide reserved procurement arrangement. I thought the Procurement Act doesn't apply to us as a devolved Scottish authority — does it apply here because we're procuring jointly with an English body?

conditional_regimes: Public Contracts (Scotland) Regulations 2015 for wholly-Scottish, non-reserved procurements

evidence_requirements.description: As a baseline under PA2023, a devolved Scottish authority is an excluded authority and is not a 'contracting authority' for the Act's purposes.

PR2024 reg 47 amends s.2(5)(a) and inserts new s.115A, which is the sole source of the joint/reserved-arrangement exception bringing this scenario back within the Act — the exception cannot be found in the Act as originally enacted.

reference_answer: Yes, it does apply here. As a baseline, s.2(5)(a) PA2023 treats a devolved Scottish authority as an 'excluded authority' and therefore outside the Act's normal definition of contracting authority — which is why the assumption that the Act 'doesn't apply' generally holds. However, PR2024 reg 47 amends the Act itself to add a carve-out to that exclusion (s.2(5)(a) now reads 'except where a devolved Scottish authority carries out procurement falling within section 115A') and reg 47 also inserts new s.115A, which PR2024 reg 47's own text (also numbered 'reg 115A' in the consolidated Regulations) provides applies the Act without modification where a devolved Scottish authority carries out procurement under a reserved procurement arrangement and, as part of that arrangement, a contract is awarded jointly with a non-Scottish contracting authority (such as an English NHS trust) or by a central buying body. This exception exists only because of the secondary legislation — it is not visible from reading the Act's excluded-authority definition alone.

topic: Pre-notice supplier registration duty on the central digital platform
scenario_text: Before we publish a contract details notice on a contract we're about to award, is there anything we're required to get from the winning supplier first about their central digital platform registration and their SME status?
query: Before we publish a contract details notice on a contract we're about to award, is there anything we're required to get from the winning supplier first about their central digital platform registration and their SME status?

evidence_requirements.description: PA2023 s.87(3) requires publication of a contract details notice after entering into a notifiable below-threshold contract, but does not itself impose a pre-publication supplier-registration check.

PR2024 reg 36A is the sole source of the duty to obtain supplier confirmation of central digital platform registration (including SME/VCSE status) and its unique identifier before publishing the contract details notice.

GOV.UK central digital platform guidance explains the practical registration steps a supplier follows, including declaring SME status and obtaining the unique identifier the authority must collect under reg 36A.

reference_answer: Yes. Section 87(3) PA2023 requires a contracting authority to publish a contract details notice as soon as reasonably practicable after entering into a notifiable below-threshold contract, but the Act does not itself impose any pre-publication supplier-registration check. Regulation 36A PR2024 fills that gap: before publishing a contract details notice under s.87(3), the contracting authority must obtain from the supplier confirmation that it has registered on the central digital platform and submitted required information (including its name, contact details, and whether it is an SME or a value-driven not-for-profit that reinvests surpluses for social/environmental/cultural goals), plus its unique identifier from the platform. GOV.UK's central digital platform guidance walks through how a supplier actually completes that registration, including selecting SME status and generating the unique identifier reg 36A requires the authority to obtain.

topic: Mandatory exclusion for conviction — PCR2015 saved procurement
scenario_text: We're partway through a procurement we started under the old rules before the Procurement Act commenced. We've just discovered the frontrunner bidder's UK subsidiary was convicted of a corruption offence four years ago. Do we have to exclude them, and for how long does that kind of exclusion normally last?
query: We're partway through a procurement we started under the old rules before the Procurement Act commenced. We've just discovered the frontrunner bidder's UK subsidiary was convicted of a corruption offence four years ago. Do we have to exclude them, and for how long does that kind of exclusion normally last?

evidence_requirements.description: For a procurement commenced before 24 February 2025 and saved under PCR2015, reg 57 sets a mandatory exclusion duty for specified convictions and fixes a 5-year exclusion period, subject to self-cleaning.

The PA2023 mandatory/discretionary exclusion-ground regime (s.57 and Schedules 6-7) is a materially different, non-applicable framework for this saved procurement and must not be substituted for the PCR2015 test.

reference_answer: Because this procurement was commenced before 24 February 2025, it continues to be governed by the Public Contracts Regulations 2015 (PCR2015), saved for pre-existing procurements, and not by the Procurement Act 2023's exclusion-grounds regime. Under PCR2015 reg 57(1), a contracting authority must (mandatorily) exclude an economic operator it has established, or is otherwise aware, has been convicted of specified offences including corruption-type offences — a conviction four years ago falls inside the mandatory exclusion period. Reg 57(11) fixes that mandatory exclusion period at 5 years from the date of conviction, so on these facts the exclusion should still apply, subject to any valid 'self-cleaning' evidence the operator provides under reg 57(13)-(14) demonstrating its reliability despite the conviction.

topic: Dynamic purchasing system openness requirement — PCR2015 saved procurement
scenario_text: We're continuing to run a dynamic purchasing system that we set up before the new procurement rules came in. Do we still have to keep it open to any supplier who meets the selection criteria throughout its life, or can we now close it to new entrants like a closed framework?
query: We're continuing to run a dynamic purchasing system that we set up before the new procurement rules came in. Do we still have to keep it open to any supplier who meets the selection criteria throughout its life, or can we now close it to new entrants like a closed framework?

evidence_requirements.description: PCR2015 reg 34(2) requires a dynamic purchasing system to remain open throughout its validity period to any economic operator meeting the selection criteria.

reference_answer: As a DPS commenced before 24 February 2025, it continues to be governed by PCR2015 reg 34, not by the Procurement Act 2023's dynamic market provisions. Reg 34(2) requires that the dynamic purchasing system be operated as a completely electronic process and remain open throughout its period of validity to any economic operator that satisfies the selection criteria — it cannot lawfully be closed to new qualifying entrants partway through its life the way a closed framework can be.

scenario_text: Our council wants to award a contract to a company we jointly control with two neighbouring councils, without running a competition, on the basis that it's really an in-house arrangement. This procurement started before the new Act came in — what's the actual legal test we need to meet?
query: Our council wants to award a contract to a company we jointly control with two neighbouring councils, without running a competition, on the basis that it's really an in-house arrangement. This procurement started before the new Act came in — what's the actual legal test we need to meet?

evidence_requirements.description: PCR2015 reg 12 sets the joint-control, 80%-activities, no-private-capital test for the in-house exemption applicable to this saved procurement.

PA2023 Schedule 2, paragraph 2 is a structurally similar but legally distinct vertical-arrangements exemption that governs only Act-regulated procurements, and must not be cited in place of PCR2015 reg 12 for a saved procurement.

reference_answer: Because this procurement was commenced before 24 February 2025, the applicable in-house ('Teckal') exemption test is PCR2015 reg 12, not the equivalent PA2023 Schedule 2, paragraph 2 vertical-arrangements exemption. Under reg 12(4), the councils may award without competition if, jointly, they exercise a control over the company similar to that over their own departments, more than 80% of the company's activities are carried out for tasks entrusted by the controlling authorities, and there is no direct private capital participation in the company (subject to limited exceptions). The PA2023 Schedule 2 test is structurally similar (also an 80% activities threshold) but is a distinct provision that only applies to procurements governed by the Act — it should not be cited as authority for a PCR2015-saved procurement.

topic: Conflicts of interest duty — PCR2015 saved procurement
scenario_text: One of our evaluation panel members on a live tender (started under the old regime) has a close personal friendship with a director at one of the bidders. Is there a formal legal duty on us to do something about that, or is it just good practice?
query: One of our evaluation panel members on a live tender (started under the old regime) has a close personal friendship with a director at one of the bidders. Is there a formal legal duty on us to do something about that, or is it just good practice?

evidence_requirements.description: PCR2015 reg 24 imposes a mandatory duty to prevent, identify and remedy conflicts of interest, expressly covering personal interests that might be perceived to compromise impartiality.

reference_answer: There is a formal legal duty, not just good practice. Because this procurement was commenced before 24 February 2025, PCR2015 reg 24 applies (not the PA2023 conflicts-of-interest provisions). Reg 24(1) requires contracting authorities to take appropriate measures to effectively prevent, identify and remedy conflicts of interest arising in procurement procedures, and reg 24(2) makes clear the concept covers, at minimum, any situation where relevant staff have a financial, economic or other personal interest that might be perceived to compromise their impartiality — a close personal friendship with a bidder's director would fall within this and must be actively managed (e.g. recusal), not merely noted as good practice.

topic: Preliminary market consultations — PCR2015 saved procurement
scenario_text: Before launching a tender we started planning under the old regime, can we talk informally to a couple of specialist suppliers to help us write realistic specifications, without that being treated as unlawful favouritism later?
query: Before launching a tender we started planning under the old regime, can we talk informally to a couple of specialist suppliers to help us write realistic specifications, without that being treated as unlawful favouritism later?

evidence_requirements.description: PCR2015 reg 40 permits preliminary market consultations with market participants before commencing a procedure, subject to non-discrimination and transparency safeguards.
PA2023's own preliminary market engagement provision (s.17) is a distinct, non-applicable rule for this saved procurement and should not be substituted for reg 40.

reference_answer: Yes, provided it is handled correctly. As this procurement was planned and commenced under the pre-24-February-2025 regime, PCR2015 reg 40 applies, not PA2023's preliminary market engagement provisions. Reg 40(1)-(2) expressly permits contracting authorities to conduct market consultations before commencing a procurement procedure, including seeking or accepting advice from market participants, and reg 40(3) allows that advice to be used in planning and conducting the procedure provided it does not distort competition or breach the principles of non-discrimination and transparency — so informal specification-shaping conversations are lawful as long as safeguards (e.g. sharing outcomes with all bidders) are applied.

topic: Eco-labels in technical specifications — PCR2015 saved procurement
scenario_text: For sustainable office furniture on a tender we're still running under the pre-2025 rules, can we require bidders to hold a specific eco-label, and can we reject a bid outright just because it doesn't have that exact label?
query: For sustainable office furniture on a tender we're still running under the pre-2025 rules, can we require bidders to hold a specific eco-label, and can we reject a bid outright just because it doesn't have that exact label?

evidence_requirements.description: PCR2015 reg 43 permits requiring a specific label subject to conditions, and mandates acceptance of equivalent labels or other appropriate proof in defined circumstances.

reference_answer: You can require a specific label, but you cannot reject a bid outright just for lacking that exact label. Because this procurement was commenced before 24 February 2025, PCR2015 reg 43 applies. Reg 43(1) allows requiring a specific label as proof of environmental/social characteristics, but only if conditions are met (criteria linked to the subject-matter, objectively verifiable and non-discriminatory, set through an open/transparent multi-stakeholder process, accessible to all, and controlled by an independent third party). Reg 43(3) requires acceptance of any label proving equivalent characteristics, and reg 43(4) requires accepting other appropriate means of proof (e.g. a technical dossier) where a bidder demonstrably had no possibility of obtaining the label or an equivalent one in time, through no fault of its own.
